sections.readable_text: Consider the equation [MATH: y''-3y'-4y = 0] where [MATH: y=y(t).] If [MATH: y = e^{\lambda t}] is a solution, then what is [MATH: \lambda?]

sections.normalized_html:
Assuming [MATH: y=e^{\lambda t}] and differentiating [MATH: y] with respect to [MATH: t] gives [MATH: y'= \lambda e^{\lambda t},\qquad y''= \lambda^2 e^{\lambda t}.]

Substituting the above into our differential equation gives [MATH: λ^{2}e^{λt} − 3λe^{λt} − 4e^{λt}|= 0; e^{λt}(λ^{2} − 3λ − 4)|= 0.]

So, we have the following characteristic equation: [MATH: \lambda^2 - 3\lambda - 4 = 0]

Factoring, we get [MATH: (\lambda -4) (\lambda +1) = 0.]

Therefore, the roots of the characteristic equation are [MATH: \lambda = 4] and [MATH: \lambda = -1.]
